screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will complete four practical competencies. First, you will manage users, projects, and roles in Keystone so that teams get the right access boundaries. This matters because misassigned roles are a common source of outages and leaks. Second, you will integrate Keystone with an external identity source such as LDAP or Red Hat IdM. I’ll explain the mapping rules and the TLS checks you must run so authentication is reliable in production. Third, you will customize Horizon to match your organization’s workflows and branding while removing unnecessary administrative panels. That reduces support calls and attack surface. Finally, you will implement core security controls such as least privilege, password policies, MFA exploration, auditing, and secure communication. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can confirm competency after hands-on tasks. These skills together let you operate a secure, auditable identity layer for OpenStack.

screens.title: Keystone: users, projects, roles
screens.narratorSegment: Keystone provides three primary abstractions: users, projects, and roles. A user represents a human or service account used to authenticate. A project is a resource container that provides isolation and quotas; think of it as a workspace where compute, network, and storage resources belong. Roles define the permissions granted to a user within a specific project. For example, a user can hold an admin role in one project to manage all resources there while having only a member role in another project. This separation is important in multi-tenant clouds because it prevents global privilege escalation. A common misconception is that the admin role always implies cluster-wide control; in OpenStack, admin scoped to a project gives full control only inside that project. A concrete example: create a project named data-science, add ds-admin with an admin role in data-science only, and ds-member with member role. They will be able to manage project resources without touching other tenants. Key takeaway: assign roles at the correct scope and always verify with role listing commands. Check your assumption by attempting role-scoped operations and watching for permission denials.

keyIdea.title: Identity model clarity
keyIdea.text: Users authenticate, projects isolate resources, and roles grant scoped permissions — admin within a project is not global admin.

content.html:
Core Concept › Keystone Model
Definitions
User: an account for a person or service, used to authenticate and receive tokens.
Project: a container for resources, providing isolation and quotas between tenants.
Role: a set of permissions granted to a user within a project; scope matters.
Analogy
Think of projects as separate offices, users as employees, and roles as job titles that permit specific actions in that office only.
Concrete Example
# Create project
openstack project create data-science-project

# Create users
openstack user create --password ds_admin_pass ds-admin
openstack user create --password ds_member_pass ds-member

# Assign roles
openstack role add --user ds-admin --project data-science-project admin
openstack role add --user ds-member --project data-science-project member
Key Takeaway

Assign roles at the correct project scope and verify with role listing to avoid privilege leaks.

screens.title: Terminal demo: create users, projects, assign roles
screens.narratorSegment: In this terminal-first demonstration you'll see a safe sequence to create a project, add two users, assign roles, and verify those assignments. Start by creating the project, then create service or human users with secure passwords. Next, assign roles explicitly within the project scope. Always verify with role list commands for each user scoped to that project. A common mistake is creating users but forgetting to assign a role, which prevents the user from performing expected actions. Another mistake is assigning a global admin role where a project-scoped admin was intended. The example commands below are the canonical CLI workflow. After execution, use a role-scoped token or openstack role list --user to confirm. If you integrate an IdP later, you'll map the external group to the project role instead of re-creating accounts, but this sequence remains the verification baseline for access correctness. Try the commands in a lab with non-production credentials first, and then run the verification steps described here. keyIdea.title: Safe CLI workflow
keyIdea.text: Create project, create users, assign project-scoped roles, then verify with role list commands to ensure access is correct.

content.html:
Process Flow › CLI Sequence
Step-by-step
  1. Create the project to hold resources and quotas.
  2. Create user accounts with secure passwords or service credentials.
  3. Assign roles within the project scope, not globally unless needed.
  4. Verify assignments using role list commands and a scoped login.
Common mistake: forgetting to verify or granting admin at global scope.
Terminal Example
# Create a project
openstack project create data-science-project

# Create users
openstack user create --password ds_admin_pass ds-admin
openstack user create --password ds_member_pass ds-member

# Assign roles
openstack role add --user ds-admin --project data-science-project admin
openstack role add --user ds-member --project data-science-project member

# Verify roles
openstack role list --user ds-admin --project data-science-project
openstack role list --user ds-member --project data-science-project
Pro Tip

Run verification commands immediately after role changes and document the expected capabilities for each role.

screens.title: Integrating Keystone with LDAP or Red Hat IdM
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating Keystone with an external directory like LDAP or Red Hat IdM centralizes authentication and simplifies lifecycle management. Architecturally, Keystone acts as an authentication broker: it validates credentials against the directory and maps external attributes to Keystone users, groups, and project roles. Mapping rules determine how directory groups correspond to OpenStack projects and roles. For example, an LDAP group named data-science-admins could be mapped to the admin role within the data-science project. Practical steps include configuring the LDAP backend in Keystone, defining user and group search bases, and creating mapping expressions that transform directory attributes to Keystone constructs. A frequent operational pitfall is incorrect search bases or filters that result in no returned users. Another is TLS misconfiguration: if the LDAP server uses certificates that Keystone cannot validate, binds will fail. Always test with a known user, use verbose logs to debug search filters, and validate certificates independently. The key takeaway: integration reduces account sprawl but requires careful mapping and certificate validation to avoid authentication outages. Integrating Keystone with LDAP or Red Hat IdM means keystone validates against ldap/idm and maps groups to projects and roles; mappings and tls are the usual failure points.. In practical terms, architecture and mapping principles for external identity providers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Keystone validates against LDAP/IdM and maps groups to projects and roles; mappings and TLS are the usual failure points.

content.html:
Definition › IdP Integration
Architecture Overview
Keystone delegates authentication to an external directory and maps attributes to Keystone users and groups.
Mapping rules connect directory groups to project-scoped roles; these are the policy layer for access.
Secure communication via TLS is required for production IdP binds and searches.
Common misconception: integration automatically makes users members of projects. You must define mappings that create or map to the desired project and role.
Conceptual Mapping Snippet
# Keystone LDAP conceptual settings (illustrative)
# [identity]
# driver = keystone.identity.backends.ldap

# ldap: url, user, password, user_tree_dn, group_tree_dn
# map group to project and role using mapping expressions
Common Mistake

Using incorrect search base DNs or forgetting to trust the IdP certificate causes authentication failures.

screens.title: Configuring TLS and testing IdP connections
screens.narratorSegment: Securing the connection between Keystone and an LDAP or IdM server is essential. Start by obtaining the IdP's certificate chain and installing the CA certificate into the Keystone host trust store or pointing Keystone to a trusted bundle. Configure the LDAP URL to use ldaps or STARTTLS depending on server support. When Keystone attempts to bind, a TLS handshake verifies the server certificate; failures are common if the certificate uses an internal CA not trusted by the host. Test connectivity before enabling mappings: use an LDAP client or openssl s_client to confirm the certificate chain and then test Keystone's LDAP backend with a known user. If searches return no entries, check the user and group search bases and ensure the bind DN has sufficient read permissions. Finally, enable verbose Keystone logs temporarily to observe search filters and TLS errors. The misconception to avoid is assuming that TLS errors are permission issues; they usually show as certificate validation failures in logs. Proper testing reduces downtime during integration. Configuring TLS and testing IdP connections means validate tls and binds before mapping rules. certificate trust issues are the most common integration failure.. In practical terms, secure binds, certificate validation, and verification steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: TLS first, mappings second
keyIdea.text: Validate TLS and binds before mapping rules. Certificate trust issues are the most common integration failure.

content.html:
Process Flow › TLS & Testing
Checklist
  • Obtain IdP CA certificate and install or reference it in Keystone trust settings.
  • Choose ldaps or STARTTLS according to IdP capability.
  • Confirm bind DN has read access to user and group DNs.
  • Test with LDAP client before adding mappings in Keystone.
Misconception: permission errors often originate from failed TLS handshakes; check cert validation first.
Verification Commands
# Example: test TLS with openssl
openssl s_client -connect ldap.example.com:636 -showcerts

# Use an LDAP client to run a search and validate user DN and attributes
ldapsearch -H ldaps://ldap.example.com -D 'cn=binduser,dc=example,dc=com' -W -b 'ou=users,dc=example,dc=com' '(uid=alice)'

# Then test Keystone mapping with a known user after configuring backend

screens.title: Horizon dashboard: roles and panels
screens.narratorSegment: Horizon is the web-based dashboard that exposes OpenStack services and user workflows. It uses the user's token to determine available panels and actions based on their roles and project scope. Administrators see additional panels for system-level tasks; regular members see only the project-scoped resources. When you customize Horizon, you control which panels are available for which roles and can streamline the interface for common workflows. A practical scenario: remove or hide the 'Admin' panels for regular users so they cannot accidentally attempt administrative actions. Another useful customization is adding links to internal support pages or pre-filled launch templates for common instance types. A common error is customizing templates without testing both admin and non-admin views; this may accidentally hide necessary options for operators. The key takeaway is to plan role-to-panel mappings and test across role types to ensure no required function is lost for any user class. Horizon dashboard: roles and panels means horizon displays panels based on user token and role mappings; customize panels responsibly and test all roles.. In practical terms, where horizon surfaces identity, projects, and role-specific ui. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Horizon displays panels based on user token and role mappings; customize panels responsibly and test all roles.

content.html:
Definition › Horizon Panels
How Horizon Uses Identity
Horizon reads the user token issued by Keystone and shows UI elements according to role and scope.
Admin roles unlock system-level panels; project roles unlock project-specific actions.
Custom panels and links can be added by creating or overriding Django templates and theme assets.
Example Customization
Place theme files and update local settings to point to your theme directory. Modify headers or panels to reflect organizational needs.
# conceptual files to modify
/etc/openstack-dashboard/local_settings.py
/usr/share/openstack-dashboard/openstack_dashboard/themes/mytheme/static/mytheme/css/branding.css
/usr/share/openstack-dashboard/openstack_dashboard/templates/_header.html
Check Your Understanding

After a theme change, verify both admin and non-admin views to ensure essential functionality remains visible.

screens.title: Horizon customization trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Customizing Horizon improves usability but introduces maintenance and security considerations. On the usability side, removing unused panels and adding pre-configured workflows reduce user errors and support requests. From a security perspective, hiding administrative panels for regular users reduces accidental privilege misuse, but it should not replace proper role enforcement in Keystone. A maintenance trade-off is that deep template overrides may conflict with future Horizon updates, requiring careful patching during upgrades. A best practice is to prefer C S S and light template overrides for branding and use explicit panel configuration to control feature visibility. Another common mistake is relying solely on UI restrictions instead of enforcing role-based access control in Keystone APIs. For example, hiding a delete button in Horizon does not prevent A P I calls that delete resources if the role permit exists. The key takeaway is to use Horizon customization to guide user behavior while enforcing security at the identity and A P I layers and planning for upgrades. Horizon customization trade-offs means customize the ui to simplify workflows, but always enforce security in keystone and plan for upgrade maintenance.. In practical terms, balancing usability, security, and maintainability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Comparison › Customization Trade-offs
Usability
Simplify workflows, add internal links, and reduce cognitive load for regular users.
Security
Hide admin panels for non-admins but enforce access in Keystone; UI hiding is not a security control.
Maintainability
Prefer small template overrides and document changes to ease future upgrades and patching.
Key Takeaway

Balance usability with security and plan for maintenance. Enforce permissions in Keystone, not just in the UI.

screens.title: Security best practices for identity management
screens.narratorSegment: Security for identity and dashboard access is multi-layered. Begin with the principle of least privilege: give users only the roles they need in the projects where they operate. Strong password policies and automated account rotations reduce credential risk. Where possible, integrate MFA for administrative accounts to add a second factor beyond a password. Enable and routinely review Keystone audit logs to detect suspicious authentication attempts, failed binds, and unusual role changes. Secure communication channels between services and the dashboard by enforcing SSL or TLS on Horizon and Keystone endpoints, and ensure web servers are patched. Implement project quotas to prevent accidental or malicious resource exhaustion; quotas act as a safety valve for multi-tenant environments. A misconception is that Horizon customizations alone protect resources; they don't. Enforcement must live in Keystone and the underlying APIs. The practical test is to attempt an unauthorized operation with a role-scoped token; it should fail and produce a logged event for review. That test verifies both access control and auditing. Security best practices for identity management means combine least privilege, mfa, tls, audit logging, and quotas to protect identity and dashboard access comprehensively.. In practical terms, least privilege, password policies, mfa, auditing, and quotas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how Keystone governs identity and how Horizon provides the user-facing dashboard. Keystone is the central point for authentication, authorization, and project isolation. You will see how users, projects, and roles combine to give precise permissions in multi-tenant environments, and why integrating an external directory such as LDAP or Red Hat IdM simplifies enterprise management. We will also cover practical Horizon customizations so the portal matches organizational needs and reduces risk. The lesson shows concrete terminal commands you can run to create a project and assign roles, explains common integration pitfalls like certificate and search base mismatches, and closes with security best practices such as least privilege, MFA options, and audit monitoring. By the end you will understand what to configure, a safe sequence of steps to follow, and the checks you must run after changes. Consider how a single incorrect role assignment might expose resources and what processes you would use to prevent that.

By the end of this chapter you will complete four practical competencies. First, you will manage users, projects, and roles in Keystone so that teams get the right access boundaries. This matters because misassigned roles are a common source of outages and leaks. Second, you will integrate Keystone with an external identity source such as LDAP or Red Hat IdM. I’ll explain the mapping rules and the TLS checks you must run so authentication is reliable in production. Third, you will customize Horizon to match your organization’s workflows and branding while removing unnecessary administrative panels. That reduces support calls and attack surface. Finally, you will implement core security controls such as least privilege, password policies, MFA exploration, auditing, and secure communication. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can confirm competency after hands-on tasks. These skills together let you operate a secure, auditable identity layer for OpenStack.

This screen describes how you will practice and verify each objective. For user and project management you will perform commands to create a project, add users, and assign roles. Verification is performed with role list commands and a role-scoped login. For LDAP or Red Hat IdM integration, you will configure an LDAP backend in Keystone, define mapping rules for users and groups, and test authentication with a corporate account. Important checks include TLS certificate validation and correct search base scopes. For Horizon customization you will place theme files, update local settings, and confirm that non-admin users do not see administrative panels. Finally, for security best practices you will audit Keystone logs, confirm password policy enforcement, and prototype MFA for admin accounts. Each practice includes a small verification step so you can mark competency and avoid common pitfalls such as overly broad roles or untested directory mappings.

Keystone provides three primary abstractions: users, projects, and roles. A user represents a human or service account used to authenticate. A project is a resource container that provides isolation and quotas; think of it as a workspace where compute, network, and storage resources belong. Roles define the permissions granted to a user within a specific project. For example, a user can hold an admin role in one project to manage all resources there while having only a member role in another project. This separation is important in multi-tenant clouds because it prevents global privilege escalation. A common misconception is that the admin role always implies cluster-wide control; in OpenStack, admin scoped to a project gives full control only inside that project. A concrete example: create a project named data-science, add ds-admin with an admin role in data-science only, and ds-member with member role. They will be able to manage project resources without touching other tenants. Key takeaway: assign roles at the correct scope and always verify with role listing commands. Check your assumption by attempting role-scoped operations and watching for permission denials.

In this terminal-first demonstration you'll see a safe sequence to create a project, add two users, assign roles, and verify those assignments. Start by creating the project, then create service or human users with secure passwords. Next, assign roles explicitly within the project scope. Always verify with role list commands for each user scoped to that project. A common mistake is creating users but forgetting to assign a role, which prevents the user from performing expected actions. Another mistake is assigning a global admin role where a project-scoped admin was intended. The example commands below are the canonical CLI workflow. After execution, use a role-scoped token or openstack role list --user to confirm. If you integrate an IdP later, you'll map the external group to the project role instead of re-creating accounts, but this sequence remains the verification baseline for access correctness. Try the commands in a lab with non-production credentials first, and then run the verification steps described here. Integrating Keystone with an external directory like LDAP or Red Hat IdM centralizes authentication and simplifies lifecycle management. Architecturally, Keystone acts as an authentication broker: it validates credentials against the directory and maps external attributes to Keystone users, groups, and project roles. Mapping rules determine how directory groups correspond to OpenStack projects and roles. For example, an LDAP group named data-science-admins could be mapped to the admin role within the data-science project. Practical steps include configuring the LDAP backend in Keystone, defining user and group search bases, and creating mapping expressions that transform directory attributes to Keystone constructs. A frequent operational pitfall is incorrect search bases or filters that result in no returned users. Another is TLS misconfiguration: if the LDAP server uses certificates that Keystone cannot validate, binds will fail. Always test with a known user, use verbose logs to debug search filters, and validate certificates independently. The key takeaway: integration reduces account sprawl but requires careful mapping and certificate validation to avoid authentication outages. Securing the connection between Keystone and an LDAP or IdM server is essential. Start by obtaining the IdP's certificate chain and installing the CA certificate into the Keystone host trust store or pointing Keystone to a trusted bundle. Configure the LDAP URL to use ldaps or STARTTLS depending on server support. When Keystone attempts to bind, a TLS handshake verifies the server certificate; failures are common if the certificate uses an internal CA not trusted by the host. Test connectivity before enabling mappings: use an LDAP client or openssl s_client to confirm the certificate chain and then test Keystone's LDAP backend with a known user.
